title: Exercise 1
text: Exercise 1A car travels around a circular track at constant speed. (a) Does its kinetic energy change? (b) Does its momentum change? (c) If the car doubles its speed, by what factors do its momentum magnitude and kinetic energy change? Explain.

title: Exercise 2
text:
Exercise 2
An object that has a small mass and an object that has a large mass have the same momentum. Which object has the largest kinetic energy?

title: Exercise 3
text:
Exercise 3
An object that has a small mass and an object that has a large mass have the same kinetic energy. Which mass has the largest momentum?

title: Exercise 4
text: Exercise 4A hockey puck slides with constant velocity on frictionless ice. It has nonzero momentum. Does maintaining that momentum require a net force? Explain using the relationship between net force and the rate of change of momentum.

title: Exercise 5
text: Exercise 5An empty cart and a loaded cart experience the same constant net force for the same time. (a) Compare their changes in momentum. (b) Compare their changes in velocity. Explain how your answers agree with both forms of Newton’s second law.

title: Exercise 6
text: Exercise 6A ball moves in a circle at constant speed. (a) Is its momentum constant? (b) Does a net force act on it? Explain using the relationship between force and momentum, and identify the direction of the net force.

title: Exercise 7
text:
Exercise 7
 How can a small force impart the same momentum to an object as a large force?

title: Exercise 8
text:
Exercise 8

Football coaches advise players to block, hit, and tackle with their feet on the ground rather than by leaping through the air. Using the concepts of momentum, work, and energy, explain how a football player can be more effective with his feet on the ground.

title: Exercise 9
text: Exercise 9Two carts of different masses start at rest on a level, frictionless track. Each is pushed with the same constant horizontal force. (a) If the forces act for the same time, do the carts gain the same momentum or the same kinetic energy? (b) In a separate trial, the carts again start at rest, but the forces act through the same distance. Do the carts gain the same momentum or the same kinetic energy? Explain.

title: Exercise 10
text: Exercise 10A 0.20-kg ball approaches a wall at 5.0 m/s. In one collision it stops; in another it rebounds at 5.0 m/s along the same line. (a) Find the magnitude and direction of the ball’s momentum change in each case. (b) If the collisions last equally long, which produces the greater average net force on the ball, and by what factor?

title: Exercise 11
text:
Exercise 11

    Explain in terms of impulse how padding reduces forces in a collision. State this in terms of a real example, such as the advantages of a carpeted vs. tile floor for a day care center.

title: Exercise 12
text:
Exercise 12
Two skaters initially at rest push off each other and move in opposite directions. Each now has momentum. How can the total momentum of the two skaters remain zero?

title: Exercise 13

Under what circumstances is momentum conserved?

title: Exercise 14
text:
Exercise 14
Can momentum be conserved for a system if there are external forces acting on the system? If so, under what conditions? If not, why not?

title: Exercise 15
text:
Exercise 15
In projectile motion with negligible air resistance, horizontal momentum is conserved, but vertical momentum is not. (a) Explain this difference in terms of the forces acting on the projectile. (b) How does this illustrate the independence of perpendicular components of motion discussed in two-dimensional kinematics?

title: Exercise 16
text: Exercise 16Revisit the garden-hose scenario in Chapter 2, Exercise 17. Explain the backward push on the hose in terms of momentum transferred to the water. How is this explanation connected to Newton’s third law?

title: Exercise 17
text:
Exercise 17

Explain in terms of momentum and Newton’s laws how a car’s air resistance is due in part to the fact that it pushes air in its direction of motion.

title: Exercise 18
text: Exercise 18An astronaut is initially at rest relative to a nearby spacecraft and is holding a tool. Neglect external forces during the following action. (a) In which direction should the astronaut throw the tool to move toward the spacecraft? (b) Explain why air is unnecessary for this method of propulsion. Use conservation of momentum in your explanation.

    What physical quantities are conserved in an elastic collision?

title: Exercise 20
text:
Exercise 20
  
    Give examples of elastic (or nearly elastic) collisions from everyday experiences.

title: Exercise 21
text: Exercise 21A cart moving at 4.0 m/s strikes an identical cart initially at rest on a level, frictionless track. Consider two proposed outcomes: A, the first cart stops and the second moves at 4.0 m/s; B, both carts move at 2.0 m/s in the original direction. (a) Which outcomes conserve momentum? (b) Which conserve kinetic energy? (c) Which could describe an elastic collision? Explain.

title: Exercise 22
text:
Exercise 22
    What is an inelastic collision? What is a perfectly inelastic collision?

title: Exercise 23
text: Exercise 23A 0.50-kg cart moving at 4.0 m/s collides with an identical cart initially at rest on a level, frictionless track. They stick together. (a) Find their common final velocity. (b) Calculate the total kinetic energy before and after the collision. (c) Where can the missing kinetic energy go? (d) Why can the carts not both come to rest?

title: Exercise 24
text:
Exercise 24
    A small pickup truck that has a camper shell slowly coasts toward a red light with negligible friction. Two dogs in the back of the truck are moving and making various inelastic collisions with each other and the walls. What is the effect of the dogs on the motion of the center of mass of the system (truck plus entire load)? What is their effect on the motion of the truck?
